claim: Several sensory patches arise by progressive segregation from a common prosensory domain in the embryonic chicken and mouse otocyst.
source: Here, we show that several sensory patches arise by progressive segregation from a common prosensory domain in the embryonic chicken and mouse otocyst.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript, including immunostaining and whole-mount preparations showing the segregation process.

claim: Notch-mediated lateral induction promotes prosensory fate.
source: Notch-mediated lateral induction promotes prosensory fate.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing the effects of Notch signaling on prosensory specification.

claim: Some of the early Notch-active cells are normally diverted from the prosensory fate.
source: Some of the early Notch-active cells, however, are normally diverted from this fate
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments using the Hes5::bicolor reporter and red-to-green constructs showing that early Notch-active cells can become non-sensory cells.

claim: Increasing lateral induction produces misshapen or fused sensory organs in the chick.
source: increasing lateral induction produces misshapen or fused sensory organs in the chick.
evidence: This is demonstrated by gain-of-function experiments using the Hes5::Dll1-eGFP construct, which resulted in morphological defects including fused sensory patches.

claim: Lmx1a (or cLmx1b in the chick) allows sensory organ segregation by antagonizing lateral induction and promoting commitment to the non-sensory fate.
source: Conversely Lmx1a (or cLmx1b in the chick) allows sensory organ segregation by antagonizing lateral induction and promoting commitment to the non-sensory fate.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including overexpression experiments showing cLmx1b reduces Jag1 expression, and loss-of-function studies in Lmx1a mutant mice showing expanded sensory domains.

claim: The vertebrate inner ear hosts multiple specialised sensory organs responsible for hearing in the cochlea, and the perception of head movements and position in the vestibular system.
source: It hosts multiple specialised sensory organs responsible for hearing in the cochlea, and the perception of head movements and position in the vestibular system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about inner ear function.

claim: Each sensory organ contains a sensory patch, composed of a regular mosaic of mechanosensory 'hair' cells, and their supporting cells.
source: Each sensory organ contains a sensory patch, composed of a regular mosaic of mechanosensory 'hair' cells, and their supporting cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cellular composition of inner ear sensory organs.

claim: The morphology of the inner ear, as well as the number, type, position and shape of sensory patches that it hosts, vary greatly across and within distinct classes of vertebrates.
source: The morphology of the inner ear, as well as the number, type, position and shape of sensory patches that it hosts, vary greatly across and within distinct classes of vertebrates (Baird, 1974; Schulz-Mirbach and Ladich, 2016; Manley and Clack, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature documenting inner ear diversity across vertebrates.

claim: The inner ear of ancestral vertebrates was probably similar to that of hagfish and lampreys, with a relatively small number of sensory patches (three in hagfish) and a rudimentary vestibular system.
source: The inner ear of ancestral vertebrates was probably similar to that of hagfish (Jørgensen et al., 1998) and lampreys (Lowenstein et al., 1968; Maklad et al., 2014), with a relatively small number of sensory patches (three in hagfish) and a rudimentary vestibular system.
evidence: This claim is based on comparative anatomy studies cited in the text.

claim: A gradual increase in the number of sensory patches (up to nine in some amphibians) has led to the acquisition of new inner ear functionalities in the course of evolution.
source: In the course of evolution, a gradual increase in the number of sensory patches (up to nine in some amphibians), possibly due to the duplication and modification of pre-existing structures, has led to the acquisition of new inner ear functionalities – in particular sound detection in terrestrial vertebrates (Manley and Clack, 2004; Fritzsch et al., 2002; Manley, 2012).
evidence: This evolutionary claim is supported by citations to previous literature on inner ear evolution.

claim: The vestibular system of birds and mammals comprises three patches (the cristae) connected to the semi-circular canals, two large patches (the maculae) in the saccule and the utricle, and the smaller macula neglecta.
source: For example, the vestibular system of birds and mammals comprises three patches (the cristae) connected to the semi-circular canals, two large patches (the maculae) in the saccule and the utricle, and the smaller macula neglecta.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the vestibular system.

claim: In mammals, the auditory cochlea forms a coiled tube that contains one sensory epithelium called the organ of Corti.
source: In mammals, the auditory cochlea forms a coiled tube that contains one sensory epithelium called the organ of Corti.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the mammalian cochlea.

claim: In birds, the ventral portion of the inner ear is formed by an elongated (uncoiled) recess containing an auditory epithelium, the basilar papilla, as well as one vestibular-like sensory patch at its distal end, the lagena.
source: In birds, the ventral portion of the inner ear is formed by an elongated (uncoiled) recess containing an auditory epithelium, the basilar papilla, as well as one vestibular-like sensory patch at its distal end, the lagena.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the avian inner ear.

claim: The monotremes (the platypus and echidnas) exhibit intermediate characteristics: an elongated cochlear duct, containing an organ of Corti-like epithelium and a distal lagena, suggesting that the lagena was present in ancestral mammals, but lost in placental and marsupial mammals.
source: The monotremes (the platypus and echidnas), remarkably, exhibit intermediate characteristics: an elongated cochlear duct, containing an organ of Corti-like epithelium and a distal lagena, suggesting that the lagena was present in ancestral mammals, but lost in placental and marsupial mammals (Schultz et al., 2017; Ladhams and Pickles, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on monotreme inner ear anatomy.

claim: Developing sensory patches could form progressively by segregation from a common 'pan-sensory' domain, a process that would recapitulate the evolutionary history of the inner ear.
source: Interestingly, it has been proposed that developing sensory patches could form progressively by segregation from a common 'pan-sensory' domain, a process that would recapitulate the evolutionary history of the inner ear (Fritzsch et al., 2002; Knowlton, 1967).
evidence: This hypothesis is attributed to previous literature through citations.

claim: All sensory patches are thought to derive from so-called 'prosensory' domains, found in the anterior and posterior domains of the otocyst.
source: All sensory patches are thought to derive from so-called 'prosensory' domains, found in the anterior and posterior domains of the otocyst, the epithelial vesicle giving rise to the inner ear.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of inner ear development.

claim: The prosensory domains are characterised by expression of the Notch ligand Jagged1 (Jag1, also known as Serrate1 in the chick) and of the transcription factor Sox2.
source: The prosensory domains are characterised by expression of the Notch ligand Jagged1 (Jag1, also known as Serrate1 in the chick) and of the transcription factor Sox2, which are both required for sensory domain formation (Kiernan et al., 2001; Kiernan et al., 2006; Kiernan et al., 2005; Brooker et al., 2006; Neves et al., 2007; Cole et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies demonstrating the expression and requirement of these markers.

claim: Notch activity, induced by Jag1, promotes Sox2 expression and commitment to the sensory fate.
source: Notch activity, induced by Jag1, promotes Sox2 expression and commitment to the sensory fate (Pan et al., 2010; Daudet and Lewis, 2005; Hartman et al., 2010; Neves et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Jag1 is positively regulated by Notch, through a process known as 'lateral induction'.
source: In addition, Jag1 is positively regulated by Notch, through a process known as 'lateral induction' (Eddison et al., 2000; Lewis, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies describing lateral induction.

claim: At E2.5 in the chicken otocyst, Jag1 immunostaining is elevated in the neurosensory competent anterior domain and in the posterior domain.
source: In the chicken otocyst at embryonic day (E) 2.5 (Figure 1A), Jag1 immunostaining is elevated in the neurosensory competent anterior domain and in the posterior domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Low levels of Jag1 expression are transiently detected in a broad ventro-medial domain that extends along the antero-posterior domain of the otocyst between E2.5 and E3.5.
source: However, as previously described (Cole et al., 2000), low levels of Jag1 expression are transiently detected in a broad ventro-medial domain that extends along the antero-posterior domain of the otocyst between E2.5 and E3.5 (arrowheads in Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-B and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: At HH21-23 (E3.5-E4), a distinct cluster of Sox2/Jag1-expressing cells (the presumptive anterior crista) was located next to a larger prosensory domain.
source: In samples examined between HH21-23 (E3.5-E4), a distinct cluster of Sox2/Jag1-expressing cells (the presumptive anterior crista, based on its location and evolution at later stages) was located next to a larger prosensory domain (Figure 1E–E').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E-E'.

claim: The junctional domain between the anterior crista and the larger prosensory domain contained Sox2-positive but Jag1-negative cells.
source: The junctional domain between the two adjacent patches was slightly constricted, and contained Sox2-positive (Sox2+) but Jag1-negative (Jag1-) cells (arrowheads in Figure 1E–E').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E-E'.

claim: At HH25 (E4.5-E5), there was a marked down-regulation in Sox2 expression between the anterior crista and the prosensory domain.
source: At HH25 (E4.5 -E5), there was a marked down-regulation in Sox2 expression between the anterior crista and the prosensory domain (double arrowheads in Figure 1F–F'), and an increase in the distance separating these patches.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F-F'.

claim: At HH25, a distinct cluster of Sox2+ cells (the presumptive lateral crista) became visible at the superior edge of the prosensory domain.
source: At the same time, a distinct cluster of Sox2+ cells (the presumptive lateral crista) became visible at the superior edge of the prosensory domain (arrow in Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At HH27 (E5-E5.5), a decrease in Sox2 expression was seen at the interface of the lateral crista and the prosensory domain, whilst Jag1 was almost extinguished in this domain.
source: At HH27 (E5-E5.5), a decrease in Sox2 expression was seen at the interface of the lateral crista and the prosensory domain, whilst Jag1 was almost extinguished in this domain (arrowheads in Figure 1G–G').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G-G'.

claim: Both cristae appeared to form by progressive segregation from a larger prosensory domain (giving rise to the utricle), during which the down-regulation of Jag1 precedes that of Sox2 expression in prospective non-sensory regions.
source: Hence, both cristae appeared to form by progressive segregation from a larger prosensory domain (giving rise to the utricle), during which the down-regulation of Jag1 precedes that of Sox2 expression in prospective non-sensory regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal analysis of Jag1 and Sox2 expression patterns shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cells transfected with the Hes5::bicolor reporter in which Notch is active, or has been recently active, exhibit red and green fluorescence in their nuclei.
source: We reasoned that cells transfected with this 'molecular timer' would fall into two categories: those in which Notch is active, or has been recently active, would exhibit red and green fluorescence in their nuclei
evidence: This is based on the design of the Hes5::bicolor reporter construct and the properties of the fluorescent proteins used.

claim: Cells in which Notch had been active previously but turned off Notch activity more than 10 hr previously should exhibit nTomato fluorescence only.
source: those in which Notch had been active previously but turned off Notch activity more than 10 hr previously should exhibit nTomato fluorescence only (Figure 2B–B").
evidence: This is based on the design of the Hes5::bicolor reporter and the half-life of the destabilized GFP.

claim: Red/green nuclei belonged to cells located within the Sox2+ sensory domains.
source: Analysis of successfully electroporated samples revealed that as expected, red/green nuclei belonged to cells located within the Sox2+ sensory domains.
evidence: This is an observation from the Hes5::bicolor reporter experiments.

claim: Cells with red (but not green) nuclei were also present outside the sensory domains.
source: However, cells with red (but not green) nuclei were also present outside the sensory domains (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the Hes5::bicolor reporter experiments shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Cells with red-only nuclei outside sensory domains had lower levels of red fluorescence than those located within the sensory territories.
source: These cells had lower levels of red fluorescence than those located within the sensory territories, as expected if these cells had been Notch-active at an earlier stage of development, but subsequently switched off Notch activity (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is an observation from the Hes5::bicolor reporter experiments shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The eGFP+ cells derived from the early Notch-active cells were detected in both sensory and non-sensory territories at E7.
source: In samples allowed to develop until E7 (n = 7) and immunostained for Sox2 and Jag1, the majority of cells exhibited red fluorescence. Strikingly, the eGFP+ cells, derived from the early Notch-active cells, were detected in both sensory and non-sensory territories (Figure 2G–H').
evidence: This is an observation from the red-to-green lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 2G-H'.

claim: Notch signalling is down-regulated in a proportion of early Notch-active prosensory cells, which then switch character and differentiate as non-sensory cells.
source: Combined with results from our Hes5::bicolor reporter, these data suggest that Notch signalling is down-regulated in a proportion of early Notch-active prosensory cells, which then switch character and differentiate as non-sensory cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lineage tracing experiments using both the Hes5::bicolor and red-to-green reporters.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Notch activity in the chick otocyst upregulates and expands cLmx1b expression.
source: A previous study has shown that pharmacological inhibition of Notch activity in the chick otocyst upregulates and expands cLmx1b expression (Abello and Alsina, 2007), suggesting that Notch activity could antagonize cLmx1b/Lmx1a expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: cLmx1b expression was strongly reduced in NICD-electroporated otocysts examined 24 hr after electroporation.
source: When compared to the contralateral (left, unelectroporated) ear, cLmx1b expression, analysed by in situ hybridisation, was strongly reduced in NICD-electroporated otocysts (n = 6/6) examined 24 hr after electroporation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from NICD overexpression experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was no down-regulation of cLmx1b in otocysts transfected with a control plasmid driving expression of mRFP1 only.
source: There was no such down-regulation in any of the otocysts (n > 10) transfected with a control plasmid driving expression of mRFP1 only (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from control experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Notch activity antagonizes cLmx1b expression.
source: These results confirm that Notch activity antagonizes cLmx1b expression, and could be at least one of the factors responsible for its progressive exclusion from developing sensory patches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NICD overexpression experiments and previous literature.

claim: cLmx1b-overexpressing cells showed reduced levels of Jag1 expression at E4.5 and E7.
source: At both stages, cLmx1b-overexpressing cells, identifiable by eGFP expression, showed reduced levels of Jag1 expression (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from cLmx1b overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the case of extensive cLmx1b transfection, very large portions of the Jag1+ sensory epithelia were missing.
source: In the case of extensive transfection, very large portions of the Jag1+ sensory epithelia were missing (see for example Figure 5B–B'' and Video 1)
evidence: This is an observation from cLmx1b overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5B-B'' and Video 1.

claim: The presence of cLmx1-transfected cells resulted in sensory epithelia with very irregular boundaries.
source: and the presence of cLmx1-transfected cells resulted in sensory epithelia with very irregular boundaries.
evidence: This is an observation from cLmx1b overexpression experiments.

claim: cLmx1b antagonizes the propagation of lateral induction at sensory patch borders by interfering with Jag1 expression.
source: These data suggest that cLmx1b antagonizes the propagation of lateral induction at sensory patch borders by interfering with Jag1 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cLmx1b overexpression experiments showing reduced Jag1 expression.

claim: At E4.5, the majority of cLmx1b-overexpressing cells located inside the sensory patches retained detectable Sox2 staining in their nuclei.
source: At E4.5, the majority of cLmx1b-overexpressing cells located inside the sensory patches retained detectable Sox2 staining in their nuclei (Figure 6A–B').
evidence: This is an observation from cLmx1b overexpression experiments shown in Figure 6A-B'.

claim: At E7, cLmx1b-overexpressing cells inside the sensory patches tended to retain Sox2 expression.
source: At later stages (E7), the cLmx1b-overexpressing cells fell into two categories: inside the sensory patches, such as the utricle (Figure 6B,D'), they tended to retain Sox2 expression
evidence: This is an observation from cLmx1b overexpression experiments shown in Figure 6B,D'.

claim: At E7, clusters of cLmx1b-overexpressing cells at the border of the sensory patches were devoid of Sox2 expression.
source: at the border of the sensory patches, we observed clusters of cells devoid of Sox2 expression (Figure 6C,E–E'').
evidence: This is an observation from cLmx1b overexpression experiments shown in Figure 6C,E-E''.

claim: The ability of cLmx1b to repress Sox2 expression is context-dependent, and appears most pronounced at the lateral border of developing sensory epithelia.
source: Hence, the ability of cLmx1b to repress Sox2 expression is context-dependent, and appears most pronounced at the lateral border of developing sensory epithelia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of cLmx1b overexpression on Sox2 expression in different locations.

claim: In E14.5 bsd heterozygous mice, the different sensory organs were easily identifiable and well separated.
source: In heterozygotes, the different sensory organs were easily identifiable and well separated; in the vestibular organs, the highest levels of Jag1 were found inside the sensory cristae (Figure 7A–B').
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining of bsd heterozygous mice shown in Figure 7A-B'.

claim: The inner ear of bsd mutant mice were smaller, with a shorter cochlear duct and an abnormally shaped vestibular system.
source: In contrast, the inner ear of bsd mutant mice were smaller, with a shorter cochlear duct and an abnormally shaped vestibular system (Figure 7C–D').
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining of bsd mutant mice shown in Figure 7C-D'.

claim: In the ventral-most portion of the vestibular system of bsd mutant mice, Jag1 was expressed uniformly and at relatively high levels throughout the presumptive saccule, utricle, and posterior crista regions.
source: In the ventral-most portion of the vestibular system, Jag1 was expressed uniformly and at relatively high levels throughout the presumptive saccule, utricle, and posterior crista regions.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining of bsd mutant mice.

claim: The Jag1 domain in bsd mutant mice was directly connected to that of the cochlear duct, which was also expanded laterally.
source: Furthermore, this Jag1 domain was directly connected to that of the cochlear duct, which was also expanded laterally (arrows in Figure 7D–D').
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining of bsd mutant mice shown in Figure 7D-D'.

claim: The fused sensory domains found in the bsd mutant arise as a consequence of the formation of ectopic, Jag1-expressing sensory progenitors.
source: Only a few hair cells (identifiable by Myo7a expression) had differentiated in these samples, indicating that the fused sensory domains found in the bsd mutant arise as a consequence of the formation of ectopic, Jag1-expressing sensory progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of expanded Jag1 expression but limited hair cell differentiation in bsd mutant mice.

claim: At E8 in Lmx1aGFP/+ mice, GFP was present throughout the otocyst but it was almost completely absent from the anterior and posterior prosensory domains, expressing Sox2 and Jag1.
source: At E8 (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), GFP was present throughout the otocyst but it was almost completely absent from the anterior and posterior prosensory domains, expressing Sox2 and Jag1.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E10.5–11 in Lmx1aGFP/+ mice, the prospective utricle expressed Sox2 and Jag1, but exhibited no or low levels of GFP fluorescence.
source: At E10.5–11, the prospective utricle expressed Sox2 and Jag1, but exhibited no or low levels of GFP fluorescence (Figure 8C–C'' and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice shown in Figure 8C-C'' and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In between the prospective saccule and utricle at E10.5-11, some cells with reduced Sox2 expression but elevated GFP levels were present.
source: In between the prospective saccule and utricle, some cells with reduced Sox2 expression but elevated GFP levels were present.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice.

claim: At E12.5 in the utricle of Lmx1aGFP/+ mice, Sox2+ and GFP- cells directly abutted the GFP+ cells at the ventro-posterior edge.
source: In the E12.5 utricle (Figure 8D–D''), Sox2+ and GFP- cells directly abutted the GFP+ cells at the ventro-posterior edge
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice shown in Figure 8D-D''.

claim: At E12.5, cells with reduced GFP and low or no Sox2 expression were present at the utricle border facing the developing anterior and lateral cristae.
source: however, cells with reduced GFP and low or no Sox2 expression were present at the utricle border facing the developing anterior and lateral cristae.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice.

claim: At E12.5, some of the cells at the edges of both cristae and within the saccule were Sox2+/GFP+.
source: At the edges of both cristae and within the saccule, some of the cells were Sox2+/GFP+.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice.

claim: At the posterior edge of the prospective utricle, Sox2/Jag1-expressing cells and GFP+ cells were separated by a relatively smooth boundary, suggesting limited cell mixing or changes in gene expression throughout development.
source: At the posterior edge of the prospective utricle, Sox2/Jag1-expressing cells and GFP+ cells were separated by a relatively smooth boundary, suggesting limited cell mixing or changes in gene expression throughout development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of sharp boundaries between Sox2/Jag1+ and GFP+ cells.

claim: The domains of the utricle facing the cristae and the saccule exhibited some overlap or mixing between Sox2/Jag1+ and Lmx1a/GFP+ cells, suggesting dynamic changes in the expression of these genes are associated to the segregation of the cristae and saccule from the utricle.
source: In contrast, the domains of the utricle facing the cristae and the saccule exhibited some overlap or mixing between Sox2/Jag1+ and Lmx1a/GFP+ cells. This suggests that dynamic changes in the expression of these genes are associated to the segregation of the cristae and saccule from the utricle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of overlapping expression patterns in specific regions.

claim: The Lmx1aGFP/GFP knock-in allele recapitulates the previously reported Lmx1a mutant phenotypes.
source: We next compared the inner ear morphology of Lmx1aGFP/+ and Lmx1aGFP/GFP littermates at postnatal day 1 (P1) and found that this knock-in allele recapitulates the previously reported Lmx1a mutant phenotypes (Koo et al., 2009; Steffes et al., 2012; Nichols et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison with previous literature on Lmx1a mutants.

claim: Lmx1aGFP/GFP P1 mice had a cyst-like vestibular region without semi-circular canal or endolymphatic duct, and a shortened cochlear duct.
source: The Lmx1aGFP/GFP P1 mice had a cyst-like vestibular region without semi-circular canal or endolymphatic duct, and a shortened cochlear duct (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice shown in Figure 9E.

claim: In the vestibular system of Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice, the sensory patches were misshapen and fused in some locations, but GFP-expressing territories were still present in between adjacent sensory patches.
source: In the vestibular system, the sensory patches were misshapen and fused in some locations, but GFP-expressing territories were still present in between adjacent sensory patches (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Additional hair cells rows were present in the basal most turn of the cochlea in Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice, the numbers of which varied between littermates.
source: Additional hair cells rows were present in the basal most turn of the cochlea, the numbers of which varied between littermates (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice shown in Figure 9G.

claim: The expression of Jag1 remained confined to the sensory territories containing hair cells in Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice, and was not expanded medially or laterally.
source: The expression of Jag1 remained confined to the sensory territories containing hair cells, and was not expanded medially or laterally.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice.

claim: The cells adjacent to the Sox2+ domain at the lateral border of the organ of Corti in Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice had higher levels of GFP fluorescence compared to heterozygous Lmx1aGFP/+ littermates.
source: However the cells adjacent to the Sox2+ domain at the lateral border of the organ of Corti had higher levels of GFP fluorescence compared to heterozygous Lmx1aGFP/+ littermates (compare Figure 9C–D and G–H), suggesting an abnormal differentiation of the Claudius and Hensen cells.
evidence: This is an observation from comparison of Lmx1aGFP/GFP and Lmx1aGFP/+ mice shown in Figure 9C-D and G-H.

claim: In the absence of Lmx1a function, some of the cells that would normally form the (non-sensory) boundary between the utricle and the crista might be diverted towards a sensory fate.
source: This suggests that in the absence of Lmx1a function, some of the cells that would normally form the (non-sensory) boundary between the utricle and the crista might be diverted towards a sensory fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of ectopic GFP- hair cells in the non-sensory domain of Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice.

claim: In the vestibular system of E15 Lmx1aGFP/+ mice, GFP+ cells were confined to the non-sensory domains separating Sox2+ sensory patches.
source: In the vestibular system of E15 Lmx1aGFP/+ mice (Figure 10A–A''), GFP+ cells were confined to the non-sensory domains separating Sox2+ sensory patches.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice shown in Figure 10A-A''.

claim: The vestibular system of E15 Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice contained expanded and abnormally shaped Sox2+ and GFP+ domains containing hair cells.
source: In contrast, the vestibular system of Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice contained expanded and abnormally shaped Sox2+ and GFP+ domains containing hair cells (Figure 10B–C'').
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice shown in Figure 10B-C''.

claim: The ectopic sensory cells in Lmx1a null animals are derived from Lmx1a-deficient cells.
source: A similar overlap between GFP and Jag1 expression was observed in the vestibular system of E14 samples (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), confirming that the ectopic sensory cells in Lmx1a null animals are derived from Lmx1a-deficient cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of overlap between GFP and Jag1 expression in Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: In E15 Lmx1aGFP/+ mice, there was a very abrupt boundary between GFP+ and GFP- cells on the medial side of the organ of Corti.
source: In the cochlear duct of E15 Lmx1aGFP/+ mice (Figure 10D–D''), there was a very abrupt boundary between GFP+ and GFP- cells on the medial side of the organ of Corti.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice shown in Figure 10D-D''.

claim: On the lateral side of the organ of Corti in E15 Lmx1aGFP/+ mice, there was a more progressive reduction in GFP fluorescence and some overlap in Sox2/GFP+ cells.
source: On the lateral side there was a more progressive reduction in GFP fluorescence and some overlap in Sox2/GFP+ cells.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice.

claim: The overlap between Sox2 and GFP on the lateral side of the organ of Corti suggests a developmental down-regulation of Lmx1a expression in the lateral domain of the organ of Corti.
source: Since this overlap was not seen in neonatal mice, this suggests a developmental down-regulation of Lmx1a expression in the lateral domain of the organ of Corti.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of embryonic and neonatal expression patterns.

claim: In Lmx1aGFP/GFP cochlea, the size of the Sox2+ domain was occasionally expanded.
source: In Lmx1aGFP/GFP cochlea, the size of the Sox2+ domain was occasionally expanded (Figure 10E–E'')
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice shown in Figure 10E-E''.

claim: At the medial border of the organ of Corti in Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice, the abrupt boundary between GFP+ and GFP- cells was disrupted and GFP+ cells were intermingled with Sox2+ cells.
source: at the medial border of the organ of Corti, the abrupt boundary between GFP+ and GFP- cells was disrupted and GFP+ cells were intermingled with Sox2+ cells
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice.

claim: At the lateral border of the organ of Corti in Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice, the gradient of GFP fluorescence was irregular, with clusters of GFP+ cells surrounded by GFP- cells in the Sox2+ domain.
source: at the lateral border, the gradient of GFP fluorescence (from high in lateral wall, to low in the Sox2+ domain) was irregular, with clusters of GFP+ cells surrounded by GFP- cells in the Sox2+ domain (arrow in Figure 10E).
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice shown in Figure 10E.

claim: The absence of Lmx1a function can lead, in a context-dependent manner, to the abnormal differentiation of cells from the Lmx1a lineage into sensory progenitors.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that the absence of Lmx1a function can lead, in a context-dependent manner, to the abnormal differentiation of cells from the Lmx1a lineage into sensory progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations in Lmx1aGFP/GFP mice showing ectopic sensory cells derived from the Lmx1a lineage.

claim: At E18 in Lmx1aGFP/+ mice, the border of the Sox2+ domain of the utricle contained cells with moderate to low levels of GFP fluorescence, intermingled with GFP- cells.
source: In samples collected at E18, the border of the Sox2+ domain contained cells with moderate to low levels of GFP fluorescence, intermingled with GFP- cells.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice.

claim: At E18, some GFP+ cells at the border of the utricle were also Sox2+, indicating their prosensory character.
source: Some of these GFP+ cells were also Sox2+, indicating their prosensory character.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice.

claim: At P42, only a few GFP+ cells were present in the Sox2+ domain of the utricle, and a mosaic pattern of GFP fluorescence was observed in the transitional cell region.
source: At P42, a stage when the utricle is considered fully mature, only a few GFP+ cells were present in the Sox2+ domain, and a mosaic pattern of GFP fluorescence was observed in the transitional cell region.
evidence: This is an observation from Lmx1aGFP/+ mice.

claim: The prolonged mosaicism in GFP fluorescence suggests the existence of a non-lineage restricted tissue boundary, where uncommitted cells can switch fate in response to cues from their external environment.
source: The prolonged mosaicism in GFP fluorescence suggests the existence of a non-lineage restricted tissue boundary, where uncommitted cells can switch fate (in this case lose Lmx1a expression and acquire a sensory character) in response to cues from their external environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of prolonged mosaic GFP expression at the utricle border.

claim: The mosaicism at the utricle border was more pronounced at the border facing the crista than at other locations of the utricle, suggesting that distinct types of sensory/non-sensory tissue boundaries are present within this organ.
source: This mosaicism was more pronounced at the border facing the crista than at other locations of the utricle, suggesting that distinct types of sensory/non-sensory tissue boundaries are present within this organ.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential patterns of GFP expression at different borders of the utricle.

claim: Lateral induction mediated by Jag1/Notch signalling plays an important role in regulating sensory patch segregation.
source: We propose that lateral induction mediated by Jag1/Notch signalling plays an important role in regulating sensory patch segregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain-of-function experiments showing that increased lateral induction affects sensory patch boundaries and can cause fusion.

claim: Lateral induction must be dampened in some of the prospective non-sensory cells to permit sensory patch segregation.
source: Another implication of these gain-of-function experiments is that lateral induction must be dampened in some of the prospective non-sensory cells to permit sensory patch segregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that increased lateral induction disrupts normal sensory patch segregation.

claim: Lmx1a is one of the factors required for the attenuation of lateral induction.
source: We found that Lmx1a is one of the factors required for the attenuation of lateral induction: the absence of Lmx1a results in expanded Jag1+ territories in the Bsd mouse vestibular system, whilst the overexpression of cLmx1b in the chick inner ear reduces Jag1 expression and results in misplaced sensory patch borders.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from both loss-of-function (bsd mutant) and gain-of-function (cLmx1b overexpression) experiments.

claim: The early sensory-competent domains, at least as defined by Sox2 expression and Notch activity, are not lineage-restricted compartments of cells with a fixed identity.
source: In summary, it is possible that some strict boundaries do form at an early stage of otic development, but the early sensory-competent domains, at least as defined by Sox2 expression and Notch activity, are not lineage-restricted compartments of cells with a fixed identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from lineage tracing experiments showing that early Notch-active and Sox2-expressing cells can give rise to both sensory and non-sensory derivatives.

claim: The early sensory-competent domains contain labile, bi-potent cells, which are sensory competent but not necessarily committed to the sensory fate.
source: Instead, these domains contain labile, bi-potent cells, which are sensory competent but not necessarily committed (Slack, 1991) to the sensory fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that early sensory-competent cells can switch to non-sensory fates.

claim: The transitional cells of the neonatal (but not the adult) utricle are capable of differentiating into hair cells after Atoh1 induction.
source: The transitional cells of the neonatal (but not the adult) utricle are also capable of differentiating into hair cells after Atoh1 induction (Gao et al., 2016), indicating that these cells are not fully committed to a non-sensory cell fate at this stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The hair cells produced at the edge of the neonate mouse utricle are not derived from early-specified and Sox2-expressing prosensory cells, but perhaps from cells of the Lmx1a-lineage that convert into sensory progenitors at later stages of development.
source: Our results suggest that the hair cells produced at the edge of the neonate mouse utricle (Burns et al., 2012) are not derived from early-specified and Sox2-expressing prosensory cells, but perhaps from cells of the Lmx1a-lineage that convert into sensory progenitors at later stages of development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of prolonged Lmx1a expression and gradual conversion to sensory fate at the utricle border.

claim: The labile character of the early sensory-competent progenitors could have facilitated the emergence of new inner ear organs and their functional diversification in the course of evolution.
source: Our findings highlight the dynamic nature of sensory patch formation and the labile character of the sensory-competent progenitors, which could have facilitated the emergence of new inner ear organs and their functional diversification in the course of evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings about the labile nature of sensory progenitors.
